paragraphs: This paper examines supervised learning when many input features are irrelevant to prediction. Its central question is how the number of training examples needed for effective learning changes as irrelevant features accumulate. Focusing on logistic regression, it compares the implications of L1 regularization with those of methods whose behavior is invariant to rotations of the feature space.

For L1-regularized logistic regression, the authors show that sample complexity grows only logarithmically with the number of irrelevant features. This matches the best known feature-selection bounds described in the abstract. The result indicates that effective learning can remain possible even when the number of irrelevant features is exponential in the number of training examples.

The contrasting result is a worst-case lower bound: rotationally invariant algorithms require sample complexity that grows at least linearly with irrelevant features. The abstract includes L2-regularized logistic regression, SVMs, and neural networks trained by backpropagation in this comparison. This is a theoretical distinction about vulnerability to irrelevant dimensions, not a claim that L1 wins on every dataset.
icml-2004-feature-selection-l1-vs-l2-reg.tldr: L1-regularized logistic regression has logarithmic sample complexity in irrelevant features, while rotationally invariant methods face a linear worst-case lower bound.

paragraphs: The paper brings together two approaches intended to help reinforcement learning handle large problems: breaking a task into a hierarchy and learning a model of the environment. Hierarchical decomposition offers a way to exploit the structure of a problem. Model-based learning addresses a complementary concern, the relative scarcity of experience available in large environments.

The proposed algorithm, R-maxq, integrates the exploration approach of R-max with the abstraction opportunities of MAXQ. The contribution is their combination within the standard reinforcement learning setting. Rather than treating hierarchy and model learning as separate options, the algorithm is designed to use both as parts of the same learning procedure.

The authors analyze sample complexity, connecting the method to questions about how much experience learning requires. Experiments in a standard simulation environment illustrate advantages of combining hierarchies with models. These findings support the proposed integration in that setting, while the abstract’s discussion of real-world scalability remains a motivation rather than a reported deployment result.
icml-2008-hierarchical-model-based-reinf.tldr: R-maxq combines R-max’s model-based exploration with MAXQ’s hierarchical abstraction, supported by sample-complexity analysis and simulation experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to approximately diagonalize several square matrices together, including matrices that are not symmetric. The aim is to identify shared eigenvector structure while estimating the eigenvalues associated with the individual matrices. Finding this common structure connects the matrices through a shared representation instead of analyzing each one independently.

The authors formulate the problem in a fully Bayesian way and derive a Gibbs sampler for the common eigenvectors and eigenvalues. The sampler provides the computational procedure for inference under that formulation. Evaluations on several datasets compare it with other joint diagonalization algorithms, with the abstract reporting performance at the state of the art.

The sampling output also supports a model-size calculation: the authors use BIC to estimate log marginal likelihood and report correctly identifying the number of common eigenvectors. This is a demonstrated result, not a universal guarantee of correct selection. Applications to blind source separation, common principal component analysis, and common spatial pattern analysis show the range of problems addressed by the same procedure.
icml-2012-a-bayesian-approach-to-approxi.tldr: A Bayesian Gibbs sampler estimates shared eigenvectors across square matrices and achieves reported state-of-the-art joint diagonalization performance.

paragraphs: The paper tackles L1-regularized least squares, a problem used in sparse recovery and compressed sensing. The objective encourages solutions with few nonzero entries, but it is not strongly convex. As a result, standard proximal gradient methods have only sublinear convergence guarantees for this problem, motivating a different way to organize the optimization.

The proposed approach solves a sequence of problems whose regularization parameters gradually decrease. This homotopy strategy still uses proximal gradient steps, but follows a path through related optimization problems. Under common compressed-sensing assumptions, the authors show that every iterate on this path remains sparse and that the objective behaves as strongly convex along the path.

That path-specific property is what enables a global geometric convergence rate for the overall procedure. The result does not require claiming that the objective becomes strongly convex everywhere; the useful curvature is established where the algorithm travels, under the stated assumptions. Empirical results support the theoretical analysis, linking the faster convergence guarantee to observed behavior.
icml-2012-a-proximal-gradient-homotopy-m.tldr: A decreasing-regularization strategy gives proximal gradient sparse recovery global geometric convergence under common compressed-sensing assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper develops an adaptive approach to canonical correlation analysis, or CCA, by expressing the problem on matrix manifolds. Its focus is the geometry of the matrices involved in the optimization. The matrix constraints are part of the mathematical setting in which the algorithm operates, making their treatment central to the proposed formulation.

A matrix manifold provides a structured space for matrices that satisfy the relevant constraints. The authors use this viewpoint because it offers a natural way to handle those constraints and tools for constructing efficient algorithms. The framework is intended to remain useful in an adaptive setting, so the contribution connects the constrained formulation directly to an updating procedure for CCA.

The paper proposes an adaptive CCA algorithm and applies it to detecting changes in EEG signals. This application gives the formulation a concrete signal-analysis use: CCA is incorporated into a change-detection problem. The stated contribution is the combination of a geometric formulation, an adaptive algorithm, and that application; the abstract does not make a comparative accuracy or speed claim.
icml-2012-adaptive-canonical-correlation.tldr: The paper formulates CCA on matrix manifolds and develops an adaptive algorithm applied to change detection in EEG signals.

paragraphs: This paper studies kernel mean matching, or KMM, in a particular covariate-shift problem. The motivation is a mismatch between the probability distributions producing training and test samples. Such a mismatch can introduce sampling bias, so the analysis asks how reliably KMM can estimate the quantity of interest when that bias must be corrected.

The authors derive confidence bounds that hold with high probability for the KMM estimator. Its convergence rate depends on two ingredients: a regularity measure of the regression function and a capacity measure of the kernel. Thus, the analysis ties estimation performance to properties of both the underlying prediction relationship and the kernel used by the method.

The paper also compares KMM with a natural plug-in estimator and establishes an advantage for KMM in the problem under study. This comparison supplies a theoretical explanation for KMM’s effectiveness, beyond simply observing that it can work in practice. The conclusion is tied to the particular covariate-shift setting and the quantities appearing in the bounds, rather than asserting superiority under every distribution mismatch.
icml-2012-analysis-of-kernel-mean-matchi.tldr: The paper bounds KMM’s estimation error under a particular covariate shift and establishes an advantage over a natural plug-in estimator.

paragraphs: The paper addresses automatic brush-stroke generation for Sumi-e ink painting. Computer simulation of this style must deal with complex scene information while producing strokes that appear smooth and natural. The authors focus on finding suitable brush trajectories automatically, turning stroke generation into a learning problem with an explicit objective.

Their approach treats the brush as a reinforcement learning agent. A policy determines its behavior, and policy search seeks brush trajectories that maximize accumulated reward. The paper also designs the agent’s states, actions, and rewards specifically for Sumi-e. These choices connect the learning procedure to the painting task: they define the situations the agent represents, the actions it can take, and what the objective favors.

Experiments with simulated Sumi-e demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The stated evidence concerns learning brush behavior in simulation. The broader contribution is a task-specific formulation of artistic motion generation: desired strokes are sought through reward-driven policy learning, with the brush trajectory itself as the behavior being optimized.
icml-2012-artist-agent-a-reinforcement-l.tldr: Artist Agent learns Sumi-e brush trajectories through reinforcement learning with painting-specific states, actions, and rewards.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a low-rank clustering method that goes beyond conventional matrix factorization. Its approximation is built from probabilities of assigning data points to clusters. The underlying construction is a two-step random walk through virtual cluster nodes, giving the low-rank representation a direct connection to the cluster assignments the method is trying to learn.

The authors measure approximation error using Kullback-Leibler divergence. They show that minimizing this error is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood of a discriminative model. This equivalence gives the objective a probabilistic interpretation: improving the approximation also corresponds to fitting that model, rather than relying only on an algebraic reconstruction criterion.

Optimization uses a relaxed Majorization-Minimization algorithm, described as helpful for finding good local minima. The version regularized with a Dirichlet prior serves only to initialize the method. Experiments report strong clustering purity across several datasets, especially large-scale manifold data. These results support the assignment-based construction empirically, while the optimization claim concerns good local solutions rather than guaranteed global optimality.
icml-2012-clustering-by-low-rank-doubly-.tldr: A clustering method builds low-rank approximations from assignment probabilities and reports strong purity, especially on large-scale manifold data.

paragraphs: The paper studies multivariate regression when observations naturally belong to groups and each group needs its own regression matrix. The challenge is to share useful information across groups while preserving differences in their predictive relationships. A single common model would not express those differences, whereas the proposed approach explicitly combines shared components with group-specific choices.

The method learns a dictionary of low-rank parameter matrices across all groups. Each group’s regression matrix is then represented as a sparse linear combination of dictionary elements. The dictionary supplies reusable structure, while the sparse combination lets each group use only selected components. The authors call this conditional sparse coding because the coding concerns response vectors given their covariate vectors.

The paper provides an algorithm and analyzes theoretical properties related to predictive accuracy. Simulation experiments compare the method with reduced-rank regression. The abstract does not specify a winning result from that comparison; its central contribution is a structured way to learn related regression models jointly, using sparse coding to balance common information with variation between groups.
icml-2012-conditional-sparse-coding-and-.tldr: Conditional sparse coding learns grouped regression models as sparse combinations of a shared dictionary of low-rank parameter matrices.

paragraphs: This paper studies transcription of telephone conversations using context-dependent deep neural network hidden Markov models, abbreviated CD-DNN-HMMs. The proposed system combines three ingredients: neural-network HMMs, context-dependent acoustic modeling, and deep-belief-network pre-training. The contribution lies in bringing these components together within a speech-recognition model evaluated on conversational audio.

The comparison is with conventional context-dependent HMM systems that use Gaussian mixture models. Both approaches retain context-dependent acoustic modeling and the HMM framework, while the proposed combination incorporates deep neural networks and their pre-training. This makes the reported result evidence for the combined modeling approach; the abstract does not separately attribute the improvement to each component.

On the demanding benchmark of speaker-independent, single-pass telephone-conversation transcription, the authors report word error rate reductions of up to one third. That is a relative reduction in the stated error measure, with one third describing the upper end of the reported improvement. The finding demonstrates a substantial advantage over the conventional comparison system on this particular transcription task.
icml-2012-conversational-speech-transcri.tldr: Context-dependent deep neural network HMMs reduce word error rate by up to one third on a telephone-conversation transcription benchmark.

paragraphs: Multitask learning can suffer when it shares information between tasks that are not meaningfully related. Discovering task clusters helps address this problem, but assigning one relationship structure to whole tasks can still be restrictive. This paper instead allows relationships to vary by feature, so tasks can be grouped differently for different parts of their models.

The proposed formulation constructs feature-specific task clusters from interactions between tasks and features. It does not require the number of clusters to be specified beforehand. This makes sharing more flexible: a relationship found for one feature need not dictate how tasks relate for every other feature. The formulation is strongly convex and can be solved efficiently using accelerated proximal methods.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets examine different degrees of task relatedness. The method’s accuracy is consistently among the best in those evaluations, rather than being claimed as uniformly best. Its learned feature-specific clusters also agree with known or plausible task structures, suggesting that the flexible relationships can provide interpretable information alongside predictive performance.
icml-2012-convex-multitask-learning-with.tldr: A strongly convex multitask method learns different task clusters for different features without requiring a preset cluster count.

paragraphs: This paper addresses feature selection in very high-dimensional data, where useful predictors may belong to correlated groups. It distinguishes two outputs: Support Features, which form a discriminative and uncorrelated subset, and Affiliated Features, which are correlated features associated with each support feature. The aim is to obtain a useful prediction subset while also revealing the surrounding feature structure.

The method incorporates correlation measures directly as constraints and uses a cutting-plane strategy for efficient embedded feature selection. The authors describe it as identifying the optimal support subset under its formulation. During the same learning process, it also discovers the affiliated groups without additional cost, making group discovery part of selection rather than a separate analysis.

The paper reports significant prediction improvements over the state-of-the-art feature-selection methods included in its comparisons. Affiliated features contribute interpretation by exposing related variables around each selected support feature. Extensive studies on synthetic and very high-dimensional real-world datasets support the method’s validity and efficiency, grounding both its predictive and structural claims in the evaluated settings.
icml-2012-discovering-support-and-affili.tldr: The method selects discriminative, uncorrelated support features while discovering their correlated affiliates without additional cost during learning.

paragraphs: This paper introduces distributed tree kernels as a way to reduce the computational and storage costs of tree-kernel methods. The underlying representations concern fragments of trees, but the proposed method embeds those feature spaces into low-dimensional vector spaces. This gives tree comparisons a compact numerical representation on which kernel computation can operate directly.

The authors provide a linear-complexity algorithm for computing tree vectors. Once those vectors are available, a kernel value is calculated with a dot product. The contribution therefore connects a representation change with a simpler comparison operation: tree-fragment information is carried into vectors, and comparisons are performed in that lower-dimensional space.

The reported results address both efficiency and preservation of useful behavior. Distributed tree kernels are faster, their values correlate with tree-kernel values, and they achieve statistically similar performance on two natural language processing tasks. Correlation does not imply exact reproduction of the original kernel. The evidence instead supports a computationally cheaper representation that retains comparable task performance in the two evaluated applications.
icml-2012-distributed-tree-kernels-fb734.tldr: Distributed tree kernels use compact vectors and dot products to accelerate tree comparisons while retaining statistically similar performance on two NLP tasks.

paragraphs: The paper develops an efficient computational building block for learning with combined sparsity constraints. Specifically, it finds the Euclidean projection onto the intersection of an L1 norm ball and an L1,q norm ball, with q equal to 2 or infinity. The projection seeks the nearest vector satisfying both constraints, an operation needed repeatedly by projection-based learning algorithms.

The authors prove that this projection problem reduces to finding a root of an auxiliary function that is monotonic and piecewise smooth. Those properties make bisection sufficient. They give time complexities of O(n + g log g) for q = 2 and O(n log n) for q = infinity, where n is vector dimension and g counts disjoint groups.

Experiments confirm the stated complexity and report substantial improvements in runtime and memory use over classical methods. The paper also evaluates the operator inside projection-based regression algorithms with composite norm constraints. Those experiments show more efficient solutions and superior accuracy relative to the compared methods, connecting the faster primitive to benefits in complete learning procedures.
icml-2012-efficient-euclidean-projection.tldr: The paper reduces projection onto combined sparsity constraints to a bisection problem, with proven complexity and empirical runtime and memory gains.

paragraphs: GroupSpAM addresses variable selection in nonparametric additive models when prior knowledge groups related covariates together. The objective is to encourage variables within a group to be selected jointly. This combines two capabilities that the abstract describes as separate in earlier approaches: group sparsity in parametric models and variable selection in flexible additive models.

The method extends the L1/L2 penalty to Hilbert spaces, allowing the sparsity penalty to act on functions grouped together rather than only on finite parameter vectors. The authors derive a thresholding condition for determining sparsity at the group level. They also provide an efficient block coordinate descent algorithm for computing the model estimate.

In simulations with additive models, GroupSpAM substantially outperforms competing methods in both support recovery and prediction accuracy. These outcomes concern identifying relevant variables as well as predicting responses. The paper also includes a comparative experiment on a real breast cancer dataset. Its contribution is a way to use known group structure while preserving the flexibility of nonparametric additive modeling.
icml-2012-group-sparse-additive-models-b.tldr: GroupSpAM combines nonparametric additive modeling with group-level variable selection and reports improved support recovery and prediction in simulations.

paragraphs: The paper addresses slow exploration in contextual bandit recommender systems with large feature spaces. Its starting intuition is that a coarse, low-dimensional description may already capture much of a user’s preferences. Exploring that simpler description can be efficient, while more detailed features can be explored when they become necessary.

The authors encode this prior knowledge in a coarse-to-fine hierarchy and introduce an algorithm that explores across its levels. The approach is meant to reduce the exploration required without committing exclusively to the coarse representation. Its performance guarantees depend on how well the coarser feature space represents the user’s preferences, making the quality of that representation an explicit part of the theoretical result.

Extensive simulations and a live user study in personalized news recommendation show substantial improvements over conventional bandit algorithms. These findings support the practical value of using a hierarchy to organize exploration in the evaluated setting. The theory also explains why the benefit is conditional: a coarse space that captures preferences well provides a stronger basis for efficient exploration.
icml-2012-hierarchical-exploration-for-a.tldr: Hierarchical contextual bandits reduce exploration by using coarse preference representations first, with guarantees tied to how well those representations fit users.

paragraphs: This paper tackles two obstacles to using low-rank kernel decompositions in changing, task-specific settings. Many existing methods do not use side information such as class labels, and their factors are tied to the samples already present. The authors seek a decomposition that can reflect the learning task and also produce factors for newly arriving samples.

Their approach generalizes the Nyström method using a flexible nonparametric structure. Priors or side information can influence the decomposition, while the learned construction generalizes the low-rank factors to arbitrary new samples. These capabilities connect the approximation to supervised information and give it an inductive character, addressing the inconvenience of a factorization restricted to the original data.

The method has linear time and space complexities. The abstract states that it can be orders of magnitude faster than existing approaches, rather than claiming that speedup in every situation. Empirical results support its efficacy and efficiency. The contribution combines task-aware decomposition, extension to new samples, and computational scalability within one low-rank kernel method.
icml-2012-improved-nystrom-low-rank-deco.tldr: A generalized Nyström method incorporates side information and extends low-rank kernel factors to new samples with linear time and space complexity.

paragraphs: InfTucker extends tensor decomposition for multiway data beyond multilinear factorization. The paper is motivated by difficulties modeling complex interactions, varied data types, noisy observations, and outliers with popular decompositions such as Tucker and CP. It proposes nonparametric Bayesian latent models that perform Tucker decomposition in an infinite feature space.

The models use latent Gaussian or t processes with nonlinear covariance functions. This provides a probabilistic approach to representing interactions, and the framework handles both continuous and binary observations. The infinite-feature formulation is paired with tensor-specific variational inference, making computation an explicit part of the contribution rather than leaving the richer representation without an efficient learning procedure.

Compared with a classical implementation, the inference technique reduces both time and space complexities by several orders of magnitude. Experiments on chemometrics and social network datasets report significantly higher prediction accuracy than leading tensor decomposition approaches. The reported findings therefore support both the computational design and the predictive usefulness of the models on the evaluated data.
icml-2012-infinite-tucker-decomposition-.tldr: InfTucker combines nonlinear Bayesian tensor models with efficient variational inference and reports improved prediction on chemometrics and social network data.

paragraphs: The paper develops Bayesian regression for count data while addressing the computational difficulty of posterior inference. Its lognormal and gamma mixed negative binomial model has two free parameters for two forms of dispersion, unlike conventional Poisson models. It also accommodates prior information, including preferences for sparse regression coefficients.

The formulation places a gamma prior on the negative binomial dispersion parameter r and connects a lognormal prior with the logit of its probability parameter p. To obtain tractable inference, the authors use a compound Poisson representation and Pólya-Gamma data augmentation. These constructions create conditional conjugacy, allowing closed-form updates within both Gibbs sampling and variational Bayes procedures.

Closed-form updates make the Bayesian computation more routine; the claim concerns the update steps rather than a closed-form solution for the entire posterior. The authors also describe the approach as readily generalizable to more complex settings with multivariate dependence. Real examples illustrate the algorithms, connecting a more flexible count model with practical inference procedures.
icml-2012-lognormal-and-gamma-mixed-nega.tldr: A mixed negative binomial count model supports two forms of dispersion and efficient Bayesian inference through closed-form conditional updates.

paragraphs: This paper studies prediction of unseen links in social networks and relational data. It combines maximum-margin learning with Bayesian nonparametrics to discover latent features that discriminate between link outcomes. The formulation also infers the unknown latent social dimension automatically, making the size of the hidden representation part of learning.

The method minimizes hinge loss using a linear expectation operator. This enables efficient posterior inference without requiring a highly nonlinear link likelihood function. A fully Bayesian formulation also avoids tuning regularization constants. Together, these choices connect a prediction-oriented margin objective with Bayesian inference over the latent representation and its complexity.

Experiments on real datasets appear to show benefits from both maximum-margin learning and fully Bayesian nonparametric inference. The abstract presents this evidence cautiously, so it supports a promising combination rather than an unconditional superiority claim. The central contribution is a link-prediction model that learns discriminative hidden features, adapts their dimension, and offers an inference route built around the margin-based objective.
icml-2012-max-margin-nonparametric-laten.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric maximum-margin model learns discriminative latent features and their dimension for link prediction.

paragraphs: The paper studies output coding for multi-label prediction, where an input can have several labels at once. A useful encoding must satisfy two goals: distinct label combinations should have well-separated codewords, and those codewords should be predictable from the input. Separation alone is insufficient if the prediction model cannot reliably produce the resulting codes.

The authors introduce a maximum-margin formulation that captures both discrimination and predictability, then reformulate it as metric learning. This creates exponentially many constraints, a computational challenge familiar from structured prediction. Because the problem lacks a label structure that makes inference tractable, the method combines relaxation techniques with cutting-plane optimization.

Experiments on image, text, and music classification show the proposed coding scheme outperforming a variety of existing multi-label prediction methods. These results support designing codes around both label separation and learnability in the evaluated applications. The contribution includes an optimization strategy for handling the large constraint set, making the joint design objective computationally usable.
icml-2012-maximum-margin-output-coding-e.tldr: Maximum Margin Output Coding learns multi-label codes that are both distinguishable and predictable, with reported gains across image, text, and music tasks.

paragraphs: The paper develops latent feature modeling for images containing multiple objects that can appear in different locations. Existing models may ignore these location changes or require images to be segmented beforehand. The transformed Indian buffet process already offers transformation-invariant features for simple, unsegmented binary images, but its assumptions and computational demands hinder its use with real images.

The authors address both issues. They combine the transformed Indian buffet process with likelihoods suitable for real images, changing how observations are modeled. They also develop an inference procedure that uses cross-correlation between images and features. This links the computational method to the relationship between a candidate feature and its possible appearances in an image.

The new inference scheme is faster than existing techniques in both theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation. The authors also demonstrate discovery of reasonable components and effective reconstruction of natural images. These findings support extending the model beyond simple binary imagery, with contributions to both the observation model and the computation needed to fit it.
icml-2012-modeling-images-using-transfor.tldr: The paper adapts transformed Indian buffet processes to natural images with suitable likelihoods and faster cross-correlation-based inference.

paragraphs: This paper addresses multiple kernel learning when some training labels are incorrect. The motivation is that many earlier methods assume perfectly labeled examples while concentrating on computational efficiency. Applying those methods directly to noisy labels can produce suboptimal performance because the class assignments guiding learning are themselves unreliable.

The authors express the noisy-label learning problem through stochastic programming and derive a minimax formulation. They then develop an efficient algorithm for the resulting convex-concave optimization problem. This makes label noise part of the learning formulation rather than continuing to optimize under an assumption that every observed label is correct.

The optimization algorithm has a convergence rate of O(1/T), where T is the iteration count. This is a statement about optimization progress, not a matching rate for prediction accuracy or label correction. Experiments on UCI datasets support both the effectiveness of the learning framework and the efficiency of its solver. The paper thus connects a noise-aware modeling objective with a computational method backed by a convergence guarantee.
icml-2012-multiple-kernel-learning-from-.tldr: A stochastic minimax formulation makes multiple kernel learning noise-aware and admits an efficient solver with O(1/T) convergence.

paragraphs: The paper examines a computational bottleneck in Bayesian network structure learning: searching an enormous space of possible networks while repeatedly scoring candidates against the observed data. The number of network structures grows super-exponentially with the number of variables. Even a search strategy that visits only some candidates can spend substantial time computing their exact scores.

The proposed approach uses a learned proxy, such as a Gaussian process regressor, in place of the true scoring function. The proxy is trained on a selection of sampled networks. The authors justify this strategy by proving a smoothness bound for a commonly used structure-learning score, providing a theoretical basis for approximating scores across candidate structures.

On several datasets, proxy-based search obtains equivalent or better scores in a fraction of the time required by an identical search strategy using exact scores. Holding the search strategy fixed makes the comparison directly relevant to replacing expensive scoring. The result supports proxy evaluation as an effective computational shortcut in these experiments, rather than claiming exact recovery of every network score.
icml-2012-smoothness-and-structure-learn.tldr: A smoothness bound supports proxy scoring for Bayesian network search, which achieves equivalent or better scores faster in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The Greedy Miser addresses the cost of making predictions after a model has been trained. Test-time CPU use includes both running the prediction algorithm and extracting its features. The latter can vary substantially across a diverse feature set, so controlling prediction cost requires accounting for more than the model’s own computation.

The proposed algorithm incorporates feature-extraction costs during training, with the explicit aim of minimizing CPU time at test time. It is a straightforward extension of stage-wise regression and applies to both regression and multi-class classification. Its central design choice is to make the eventual cost of obtaining inputs part of how the predictor is learned.

The paper reports that Greedy Miser is significantly more cost-effective than prior work and scales to larger datasets. These findings connect a training-time decision to deployment-time efficiency: the method considers costs before the learned model is used for prediction. The contribution is a broadly applicable learning procedure for settings where feature computation is a meaningful part of the test-time budget.
icml-2012-the-greedy-miser-learning-unde.tldr: Greedy Miser accounts for feature-extraction costs during training to reduce test-time CPU use for regression and multi-class classification.
